lane: PROTOTYPE (non-canon) BMD-1 gravity steering, trajectory test
law: |a_f| <= 1.5 g_P; reaction to P; onboard energy F . v_rel(P)

torch_reference.note: explorer reference tank for Earth sea-to-orbit (R1 legs), ~minutes; jet energy ~ water x ve^2/2 = several TJ

prograde.note: speeds the orbit up: energy = F . v_helio

normal.note: rotates the velocity: a plane change costs only 1/2 m dv_n^2

verdict.landing_capability: YES: hover and slow lift near a body cost ~0 power; the 200 m exhaust-free lift is available.
verdict.torch_alternative: ALSO YES - the law as stated is not a landing aid. With only the shuttle's existing 29 MWe reactor it reaches 400 km orbit with ZERO propellant in ~19.36 h; with a torch-class 7.7 GW source in ~0.35 h. Holding altitude while gaining speed costs no power (force perpendicular to velocity), so the only bill is the orbital energy (~2 TJ). In heliocentric space it gives ~768 m/s per day to ANY ship (acceleration is mass-independent), plane changes almost free, ~8538 m/s per day at 0.3 AU.
verdict.meaning: Gravity steering as stated is a propellant-free alternative to the torch for orbit insertion and slow interplanetary freight: a setting-scale change, not a shuttle feature.
verdict.the_leak: Force perpendicular to the partner-relative velocity does no work. Any law that caps force by gravity but prices energy by F . v_rel gives free altitude-holding, free plane changes and power-limited (not propellant-limited) orbit raising.
verdict.if_landing_only_is_wanted: The capacity must fall off with distance from the partner's SURFACE (a proximity law on the scale of the domain, ~10-100 m), not with g_P. That is a different constitutive law and is not tested here.
